title: Data Analysis Practice Questions
description: Practice descriptive statistics, tables and chart interpretation, variability and quartiles, correlation and time-series direction, aggregation and filtering, data visualization, data quality and missing values, and sampling and populations. Questions use explicit statistical conventions and traceable source identifiers.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: A pie chart divides the total of monthly revenue (thousands of USD) for a store into \(4\) mutually exclusive categories covering the whole total. The known shares are Category B: \(22\%\); Category D: \(22\%\); Category A: \(21\%\). Category C is unlabeled. What percentage does Category C represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(22+22+21)=35\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded the following test scores over \(7\) periods: \(26, 55, 77, 63, 12, 69, 67\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(7\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{26+55+77+63+12+69+67}{7}\\
&= \frac{369}{7}\\
&\approx 52.71
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the first quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders (sorted): \(22, 37, 47, 49, 59, 66, 69, 76\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_1\) (the first quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the lower half is \(22, 37, 47, 49\). Its median is \(Q_1=\frac{37+47}{2}=42\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A team logged these points scored per game: \(11, 17, 21, 31, 43, 54, 98\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(11, 17, 21, 31, 43, 54, 98\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(31\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.concept: Calculating a percentage of a total
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage share of one category relative to the total.
questions.question: A table lists monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store. The regions have nonoverlapping contributions: East: \(50\); South: \(26\); West: \(33\); Central: \(86\); North: \(83\). What percentage of the total does West represent (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The total is \(50+26+33+86+83=278\). The share for West is \(\frac{33}{278}\approx 11.9\%\), rounded to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the category's value by the total, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A factory recorded these units produced per shift: \(14, 24, 26, 34, 40, 68, 86, 93\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(14, 24, 26, 34, 40, 68, 86, 93\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{34+40}{2}=37\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: An account recorded these daily new followers: \(59, 61, 74, 30, 35, 35, 35\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(35\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(35\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows customer satisfaction point totals by category for a survey: Q3: \(49\); Q4: \(197\); West: \(41\); North: \(79\). Which category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(197\), belonging to the category labeled Q4.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An account recorded these daily new followers: \(84, 32, 86, 57, 95, 67\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(32\) and the maximum is \(95\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=95-32=63\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lowest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders: \(72, 78, 88, 38, 67, 66, 82\). What is the lowest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The lowest value is \(38\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the lowest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the names of clinics in a directory. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: B
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains names or category labels, so its values are categorical. It does not contain numerical measurements or a mixture of both value types.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A logistics company recorded delivery times (hours) of \(129\) in Period \(1\) and \(152\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(152-129=23\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the type of sampling bias present in a research scenario.
questions.question: A survey about investment habits is conducted only at a stock-trading conference, asking whoever passes by. The target population is the wider community, not just people at that venue. Which sampling bias is the main concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Selection bias (the sample overrepresents people already engaged with investment)

options.label: B
options.text: No bias, since the people were approached at random moments

options.label: C
options.text: Measurement bias due to a faulty survey instrument

questions.explanation: Restricting recruitment to this venue can overrepresent people whose interests or activities are associated with it and underrepresent the wider community. This is selection bias; random timing at a restricted venue does not make the whole-community sample representative.
questions.hint: Consider whether the location or method of choosing participants favors a particular group.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores (sorted): \(20, 22, 54, 57, 66, 67, 83, 89\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{22+54}{2}=38\\
Q_3 &= \frac{67+83}{2}=75\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=75-38=37
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.learningObjective: Classify the strength and direction of a correlation from its coefficient r.
questions.question: For this exercise, classify Pearson correlation strength as weak when \(|r|<0.4\), moderate when \(0.4\le |r|<0.8\), and strong when \(0.8\le |r|\le 1\). The coefficient is \(r=-0.32\). How should this correlation be described?
questions.explanation: Using the stated exercise rubric, \(|r|=0.32\) gives the strength classification. The negative sign gives the direction, so the answer is weak negative correlation. These cutoffs are an exercise convention, not universal subject-independent thresholds.
questions.hint: Apply the stated magnitude intervals to \(|r|\), then use the sign of \(r\) for direction.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the sum of values for one group within a dataset.
questions.question: A dataset of session durations (minutes) for a website lists (region:value pairs): West: \(20\); West: \(18\); West: \(45\); North: \(37\); North: \(42\); North: \(25\); East: \(40\); East: \(52\); East: \(43\). What is the total for the North region?
questions.explanation: Keep only records in the North group. Their total is \(37+42+25=104\). Other groups are excluded from this sum.
questions.hint: Add up only the entries labeled North.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret individually plotted points beyond a boxplot's whiskers.
questions.question: On a Tukey boxplot of a team's points scored per game, several individual points are plotted separately beyond the whiskers. What do these points most likely represent? Here, whiskers stop at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.explanation: Under the stated Tukey convention, observations outside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences are flagged as outliers and plotted separately beyond the whiskers. This flag does not by itself establish a data-entry error.
questions.hint: Compare the positions of the separate points with the interval covered by the whiskers.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the correct way to calculate a mean when a value is missing.
questions.question: An account's daily new followers dataset has \(5\) entries, but one entry is missing (blank): \(23, 47, 29, 24\), [missing]. How should the mean of only the four observed values be calculated, without imputing the missing value?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat the missing value as zero: \(\frac{123}{5}=24.6\).

options.label: B
options.text: No statistic can be calculated from the observed values.

options.label: C
options.text: Use only the four observed values: \(\frac{123}{4}=30.75\).

questions.explanation: The requested statistic is the observed-data mean, so divide the observed sum by the observed count: \(\bar{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{123}{4}=30.75\). The mean of all five intended entries cannot be determined without the missing value or an explicit imputation assumption.
questions.hint: Decide which entries belong in the requested statistic and use the matching denominator.

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: An account's daily new followers has \(Q_1=49\) and \(Q_3=69\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(59\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

options.label: C
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 69-49=20\\
L &= 49-1.5(20)=19\\
U &= 69+1.5(20)=99
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(59\) lies within the two fences, so it is not an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the chart type that satisfies the explicitly stated encoding requirement.
questions.question: An analyst wants a chart for showing how a website's session durations (minutes) changed each month over \(3\) years. Which chart type connects successive monthly points with line segments to emphasize change over time?
questions.explanation: A line chart joins successive time-ordered points, making month-to-month change easy to follow. A bar chart can also display monthly data, but it does not provide the requested connected-point form.
questions.hint: Match the chart type to what's being shown: comparison, trend over time, parts of a whole, relationship between two variables, or a distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Recalculate a correct total after identifying a duplicate data entry.
questions.question: A dataset of units produced per shift for a factory accidentally contains the entry \(62\) twice due to a data-entry error: \(62, 32, 49, 66, 62\). Source records confirm that one occurrence of the repeated value is a copied record. What is the correct total after removing exactly that one duplicate record?
questions.explanation: Remove one confirmed copy of the \(62\) record. The corrected records are \(32, 49, 66, 62\), with total \(32+49+66+62=209\). Equal values alone are not sufficient grounds for deleting independent records.
questions.hint: Identify and remove the duplicate entry before summing.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the number of purchases made through a social media account each day. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: A count takes nonnegative whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a campaign lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(67, 73, 58, 59\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(67+73+58+59=257\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish between a population and a sample in a research scenario.
questions.question: A pollster surveys \(100\) randomly selected people out of a population with \(20000\) total members. Take the entire stated group of people or the entire stated batch of items as the target population. Does the inspected or surveyed set include that whole population or only a sample?

options.label: B
options.text: The population consists only of members not selected for this investigation

questions.explanation: The target population is the entire stated group. Only a proper subset is selected, so the surveyed set is a sample from that population.
questions.hint: A population includes every member of the group of interest; a sample is a subset of it.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: An online store recorded the following daily orders over \(5\) periods: \(54, 48, 42, 14, 58\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(5\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{54+48+42+14+58}{5}\\
&= \frac{216}{5}\\
&=43.20
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows delivery times (hours) for a logistics company by month: Jan: \(107\), Feb: \(61\), Mar: \(98\), Apr: \(45\). What value does the bar for Jan show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(107\) to Jan. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A class's test scores went from \(88\) to \(87\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{87-88}{88}\times 100\\
&\approx -1.1
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-1.1\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A campaign logged these click-through rates (percent): \(13, 48, 61, 65, 67, 72, 81\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(13, 48, 61, 65, 67, 72, 81\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(65\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a data quality issue caused by an inconsistent data type.
questions.question: A spreadsheet column intended to hold numeric values for 'Rating' contains the entries \(4\), \(5\), \(3\), 'good', \(2\). What is the data quality issue here?

options.label: A
options.text: The column has too many entries

options.label: B
options.text: One entry is stored as text instead of a number, which is an inconsistent data type

options.label: C
options.text: The rating values are not sorted in order

questions.explanation: The column mixes numbers with a nonnumeric text entry or missing-value marker. That entry must be identified and handled explicitly before numerical analysis. Some tools reject it; others silently omit text, so it does not necessarily cause a calculation error in every spreadsheet.
questions.hint: Look for an entry that doesn't match the expected format of the rest of the column.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks daily active user counts (thousands) for a product over five months: Jan: \(40\), Feb: \(144\), Mar: \(28\), Apr: \(70\), May: \(57\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(144\), which occurs in Feb.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A store recorded these monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD): \(13, 15, 18, 21, 31, 43, 59, 78\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(13, 15, 18, 21, 31, 43, 59, 78\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{21+31}{2}=26\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores: \(82, 12, 25, 32, 32, 79, 32\). What is the mode?

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a pie chart with many near-equal categories is difficult to compare.
questions.question: A clinic's dataset has \(18\) categories of recorded patient visits with fairly similar counts covering the complete dataset. Why would a pie chart likely be a poor choice for visualizing it?

options.label: A
options.text: Pie charts cannot display more than \(2\) categories at all

options.label: B
options.text: Too many similarly sized slices make the chart cluttered and hard to compare

options.label: C
options.text: Pie charts can only be used for numerical, not categorical, data

questions.explanation: Many near-equal slices crowd a pie chart and make small differences difficult to compare. A bar chart aligns lengths to a shared baseline, making category comparisons easier.
questions.hint: Think about how easy it is to visually compare many thin slices of similar size.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows daily active user counts (thousands) by labeled category for a product: West: \(28\); Q1: \(29\); Online: \(58\); East: \(172\); Retail: \(155\). Which labeled category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(172\), belonging to the category labeled East.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the bin with the highest frequency in a histogram.
questions.question: A histogram of app load times (seconds) for an app uses measurements rounded to whole numbers. Its inclusive integer bins have these counts: \(0\le x\le 20\): \(37\), \(21\le x\le 40\): \(13\), \(41\le x\le 60\): \(29\), \(61\le x\le 80\): \(28\), \(81\le x\le 100\): \(19\). Which bin contains the most observations?
questions.explanation: Compare the stated bin frequencies. The \(0\le x\le 20\) bin has \(37\) observations, strictly more than every other bin. The stated integer rounding removes gaps between consecutive inclusive integer bins.
questions.hint: Compare the bar heights (counts) across all the bins.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a website lists these counts across \(5\) categories: \(33, 22, 17, 19, 78\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(33+22+17+19+78=169\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: An experiment recorded these reaction times (ms): \(26, 24, 18, 22, 20\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=22\). The squared deviations sum to \(40\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{40}{5}=8\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{8}\approx 2.83
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(97, 16, 25, 89, 83, 52\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(16\) and the maximum is \(97\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=97-16=81\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Count how many observations in a dataset satisfy a filter condition.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores for \(10\) observations: \(42, 87, 37, 51, 34, 54, 72, 44, 62, 28\). How many observations are greater than \(60\)?
questions.explanation: The values satisfying the strict condition \(x>60\) are \(87, 72, 62\). There are \(3\) such observations.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: An online store recorded daily orders of \(145\) in Period \(1\) and \(202\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(202-145=57\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sample size given a study description.
questions.question: A researcher wants to study opinions across a population of \(10000\) people and selects \(500\) of them at random to survey. What is the sample size in this study?
questions.explanation: The selected study group contains \(500\) people, so the sample size is \(n=500\). The full population size is \(10000\).
questions.hint: The sample size is how many were actually selected and studied, not the size of the whole group.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sampling method used in a research scenario.
questions.question: A researcher studying a city surveys only the people who happen to walk by their table today. What sampling method does this describe?
questions.explanation: The researcher recruits easily available passers-by rather than using a random draw from a complete population list. This is convenience sampling; it need not reflect the target population.
questions.hint: Consider whether selection is based on a uniform random draw from a complete list, on predefined subgroups, or on availability.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a weighted mean when combining groups of different sizes.
questions.question: A store has two groups: Group \(1\) has \(37\) observations with a mean of \(50\), and Group \(2\) has \(30\) observations with a mean of \(79\). What is the overall (weighted) mean across both groups (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
Multiply each group mean by that group count, then divide the combined total by the combined count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{37\cdot 50+30\cdot 79}{37+30}\\
&= \frac{4220}{67}\\
&\approx 62.99
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Multiply each group mean by its number of observations before combining the groups.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish between a population and a sample in a research scenario.
questions.question: A quality inspector checks every single unit produced in a batch of \(50\) items for a marketing campaign. Take the entire stated group of people or the entire stated batch of items as the target population. Does the inspected or surveyed set include that whole population or only a sample?

options.label: C
options.text: The population consists only of members not selected for this investigation

questions.explanation: The target population is the entire stated group. Every member is included, so the inspected or surveyed set is the full population, and the investigation is a census.
questions.hint: A population includes every member of the group of interest; a sample is a subset of it.
