Its inclusive integer bins have these counts: \(0\le x\le 20\): \(20\), \(21\le x\le 40\): \(24\), \(41\le x\le 60\): \(39\), \(61\le x\le 80\): \(16\), \(81\le x\le 100\): \(7\). Which bin contains the most observations?
questions.explanation: Compare the stated bin frequencies. The \(41\le x\le 60\) bin has \(39\) observations, strictly more than every other bin. The stated integer rounding removes gaps between consecutive inclusive integer bins.
questions.hint: Compare the bar heights (counts) across all the bins.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(33, 64, 66, 83, 16\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(16\) and the maximum is \(83\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=83-16=67\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify stratified sampling from a described method.
questions.question: A researcher divides a factory's products into production lines, then randomly selects a proportional number of products from each production line to inspect. What sampling method is this?
questions.explanation: The researcher partitions the population into strata and randomly samples within every stratum. This is stratified sampling. Proportional allocation is the version used here; stratified sampling does not require proportional allocation in every application.
questions.hint: This method deliberately splits the population into subgroups before sampling from each one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A city's daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit) went from \(135\) to \(115\). Using the numerical Fahrenheit readings specifically, what is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{115-135}{135}\times 100\\
&\approx -14.8
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-14.8\%\). This is a percentage change of the numerical readings on the Fahrenheit scale; it is scale-dependent and is not a percentage change in absolute thermodynamic temperature.
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart

questions.explanation: The researcher recruits easily available passers-by rather than using a random draw from a complete population list. This is convenience sampling; it need not reflect the target population.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded the following daily stock closing prices (USD) over \(7\) periods: \(88, 48, 27, 80, 58, 82, 61\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?

\end{aligned}\]

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: A survey recorded these customer satisfaction point totals: \(19, 17, 21, 27, 31\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=23\). The squared deviations sum to \(136\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{136}{5}=27.2\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{27.2}\approx 5.22
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Sum values within groups and compare totals across groups.
questions.question: A survey's customer satisfaction point totals are grouped as follows — Group A: \(20, 18, 20, 26\); Group B: \(36, 29, 19, 48\); Group C: \(26, 38, 12, 32\). If you group by category and sum the values, which group has the highest total?

options.text: No statistic can be calculated from the observed values.

options.label: B
options.text: Use only the four observed values: \(\frac{153}{4}=38.25\).

options.label: C
options.text: Treat the missing value as zero: \(\frac{153}{5}=30.6\).

questions.explanation: The requested statistic is the observed-data mean, so divide the observed sum by the observed count: \(\bar{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{153}{4}=38.25\). The mean of all five intended entries cannot be determined without the missing value or an explicit imputation assumption.
questions.hint: Decide which entries belong in the requested statistic and use the matching denominator.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the third quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit) (sorted): \(16, 31, 36, 38, 40, 64, 65, 93\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_3\) (the third quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the upper half is \(40, 64, 65, 93\). Its median is \(Q_3=\frac{64+65}{2}=64.5\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: A pie chart divides the total of daily new followers for an account into \(3\) mutually exclusive categories covering the whole total. The known shares are Category D: \(13\%\); Category E: \(19\%\). Category A is unlabeled. What percentage does Category A represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(13+19)=68\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A store recorded these monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD): \(12, 22, 72, 73, 85, 88\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(12, 22, 72, 73, 85, 88\). With an even count of \(6\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{72+73}{2}=72.5\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a team lists these counts across \(5\) categories: \(13, 77, 58, 47, 65\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(13+77+58+47+65=260\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: A website recorded these session durations (minutes) (sorted): \(12, 15, 33, 51, 53, 55, 62, 94\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{15+33}{2}=24\\
Q_3 &= \frac{55+62}{2}=58.5\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=58.5-24=34.5
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: An account's daily new followers has \(Q_1=44.5\) and \(Q_3=57\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(87\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: A
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 57-44.5=12.5\\
L &= 44.5-1.5(12.5)=25.75\\
U &= 57+1.5(12.5)=75.75
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(87\) lies above the upper fence, so it is an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an observed association from an established causal relationship.
questions.question: A study finds that umbrella sales and traffic accidents both rise at the same time of year and are positively correlated. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: The observed correlation proves that the first variable causes the second

options.label: B
options.text: The correlation alone does not establish causation; rainy weather could influence both variables

options.label: C
options.text: The correlation is meaningless and should be ignored entirely

questions.explanation: The observational association alone establishes neither a direct causal relationship nor its absence. Rainy weather is a plausible common influence, but additional evidence would be needed to establish the causal mechanism.
questions.hint: Correlation between two variables doesn't prove either one causes the other — consider a third factor.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a described relationship as positive, negative, or no correlation.
questions.question: As a delivery distance increases, on-time delivery rate tends to decrease. What type of relationship does this describe?
questions.explanation: The described variables tend to move in opposite directions, giving a negative association. This describes association rather than demonstrating causation.
questions.hint: Positive: both move the same direction. Negative: they move opposite directions. No correlation: no consistent pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A campaign recorded these click-through rates (percent): \(41, 41, 25, 13, 89, 10, 41\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(41\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(41\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows daily new followers for an account by month: Jan: \(96\), Feb: \(82\), Mar: \(137\), Apr: \(32\), May: \(25\). What value does the bar for Feb show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(82\) to Feb. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.concept: Identifying net direction in time-series data
questions.learningObjective: Classify the sign of the first-to-last net change in a time series.
questions.question: A campaign's click-through rates (percent) over five consecutive periods were: \(85, 73, 73, 55, 65\). For this question, classify the direction by the net change from the first period to the last: positive means an increase, negative means a decrease, and zero means no net change. Which option describes that direction?

options.label: A
options.text: Net increase from first to last period

options.label: B
options.text: No net change between first and last periods

options.label: C
options.text: Net decrease from first to last period

questions.explanation: Using the stated endpoint criterion, \(\Delta=65-85=-20\). This is negative, so there is a net decrease. This criterion does not establish a fitted regression trend or statistical significance.
questions.hint: Apply the criterion stated in the question to the first and last observations.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks session durations (minutes) for a website over five months: Jan: \(20\), Feb: \(142\), Mar: \(124\), Apr: \(131\), May: \(143\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(143\), which occurs in May.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a groupby-and-aggregate operation produces.
questions.question: A data analyst runs `df.groupby('region')['sales'].mean()` on a sales dataset for a clinic. Assume region labels are present and sales is numeric, with at least one observed sales value in every group. What does the result represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The overall average sales across the entire dataset

options.label: B
options.text: The average sales value for each region

options.label: C
options.text: The total number of rows for each region

questions.explanation: The operation partitions rows by the region column, then calculates the arithmetic mean of observed numeric sales within each region. The resulting Series has one mean per region; it is neither an overall mean nor a row count. Missing sales values are skipped by the default mean aggregation.
questions.hint: groupby() splits the data into groups first, then the aggregation is applied within each group.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders: \(25, 27, 33, 21, 29\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=27\). The squared deviations sum to \(80\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{80}{5}=16\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{16}\approx 4.00
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two datasets using population standard deviation as the specified spread measure.
questions.question: Two portfolios recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD): Beacon: \(48\), \(49\), \(52\), \(51\), \(50\); Alpha: \(38\), \(65\), \(72\), \(30\), \(55\). Using population standard deviation to measure spread, which dataset has greater variability?
questions.explanation: The population variances are Beacon: \(2\); Alpha: \(251.6\). Taking square roots preserves their order. Therefore, Alpha has the greater population standard deviation. The comparison concerns spread, not the sizes of the means.
questions.hint: Compare distances from each dataset's own mean using the stated spread measure.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores: \(89, 12, 99, 33, 85, 59, 83\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(12\) and the maximum is \(99\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=99-12=87\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the highest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An app recorded these app load times (seconds): \(76, 28, 29, 46, 56, 87, 85, 97\). What is the highest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The highest value is \(97\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the highest one.

questions.concept: Calculating a percentage of a total
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage share of one category relative to the total.
questions.question: A table lists sums of recorded app load times (seconds) for an app. The regions have nonoverlapping contributions: Central: \(74\); West: \(78\); South: \(70\); North: \(38\). What percentage of the total does West represent (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The total is \(74+78+70+38=260\). The share for West is \(\frac{78}{260}\approx 30.0\%\), rounded to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the category's value by the total, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the number of items or events recorded each day at a store. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains counts or measured quantities, so its values are numerical. Recording these values over time does not change their numerical value type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the exact time in seconds taken by a delivery process. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: Before instrument rounding, the modeled duration or mass can vary continuously over a range. It is continuous numerical data, even though an instrument reports it to finite precision.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows units produced per shift by labeled category for a factory: South: \(73\); North: \(43\); Retail: \(166\); Q3: \(54\). Which labeled category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(166\), belonging to the category labeled Retail.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Recalculate a correct total after identifying a duplicate data entry.
questions.question: A dataset of customer satisfaction point totals for a survey accidentally contains the entry \(68\) twice due to a data-entry error: \(68, 56, 54, 75, 68\). Source records confirm that one occurrence of the repeated value is a copied record. What is the correct total after removing exactly that one duplicate record?
questions.explanation: Remove one confirmed copy of the \(68\) record. The corrected records are \(56, 54, 75, 68\), with total \(56+54+75+68=253\). Equal values alone are not sufficient grounds for deleting independent records.
questions.hint: Identify and remove the duplicate entry before summing.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for an app lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(18, 45, 60, 62\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(18+45+60+62=185\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a data quality issue caused by an inconsistent data type.
questions.question: A spreadsheet column intended to hold numeric values for 'Price' contains the entries \(52.99\), \(5.50\), 'N/A', \(9.00\), \(42.75\). What is the data quality issue here?

options.label: A
options.text: One entry is stored as text instead of a number, which is an inconsistent data type

options.label: B
options.text: The price values are not sorted in order

options.label: C
options.text: The column has too many entries

questions.explanation: The column mixes numbers with a nonnumeric text entry or missing-value marker. That entry must be identified and handled explicitly before numerical analysis. Some tools reject it; others silently omit text, so it does not necessarily cause a calculation error in every spreadsheet.
questions.hint: Look for an entry that doesn't match the expected format of the rest of the column.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a scatter plot that shows no clear pattern.
questions.question: A scatter plot of an employee's years of experience versus their monthly sales total uses two quantitative variables. Its points are scattered with no visible upward or downward linear pattern. What does this suggest about the observed variables?

options.label: A
options.text: There is little to no linear correlation between the variables

options.label: B
options.text: There is a strong positive correlation between the variables

options.label: C
options.text: One variable definitely causes the other

questions.explanation: The described scatter suggests little or no visible linear association in the observed data. It does not establish that the exact correlation is zero, rule out a nonlinear relationship, or prove causation.
questions.hint: A clear correlation would show points following a visible upward or downward pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A city recorded the following daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit) over \(6\) periods: \(38, 47, 41, 16, 90, 86\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(6\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{38+47+41+16+90+86}{6}\\
&= \frac{318}{6}\\
&=53.00
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: An app logged these app load times (seconds): \(11, 23, 32, 45, 59, 80, 85\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(11, 23, 32, 45, 59, 80, 85\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(45\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what each component of a boxplot represents.
questions.question: A conventional Tukey boxplot is drawn for a survey's customer satisfaction ratings (on a scale from \(1\) to \(10\)). Which part of the boxplot represents the median of the data?
questions.explanation: In this conventional boxplot, the line inside the box marks the median. The two box edges mark \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\). The whiskers end at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.hint: Distinguish the box interior, box edges, whisker endpoints, and separately plotted observations.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows click-through rates (percent) for a campaign by month: Jan: \(68\), Feb: \(73\), Mar: \(66\), Apr: \(59\). What value does the bar for Jan show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(68\) to Jan. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret an SQL query combining a WHERE filter with an aggregate function.
questions.question: A SQL query is written as: `SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE amount > 500;` on an orders table for a business experiment. Assume amount is numeric and at least one order satisfies the filter. What does this query return?

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of orders above \(500\)

options.label: B
options.text: The average order amount, considering only orders above \(500\)

options.label: C
options.text: The average order amount across all orders, regardless of amount

questions.explanation: The WHERE condition keeps only rows with \(\mathrm{amount}>500\). AVG then computes the arithmetic mean of those qualifying amounts, rather than averaging all orders or counting them. Without a qualifying value, SQL AVG would return NULL; the question explicitly excludes that case.
questions.hint: The WHERE clause filters rows before the aggregate function is applied.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the sum of values for one group within a dataset.
questions.question: A dataset of units produced per shift for a factory lists (region:value pairs): East: \(60\); East: \(14\); East: \(50\); South: \(16\); South: \(52\); South: \(26\); West: \(20\); West: \(20\); West: \(32\). What is the total for the East region?
questions.explanation: Keep only records in the East group. Their total is \(60+14+50=124\). Other groups are excluded from this sum.
questions.hint: Add up only the entries labeled East.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A product recorded daily active user counts (thousands) of \(56\) in Period \(1\) and \(103\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(103-56=47\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A team's points scored per game went from \(85\) to \(66\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{66-85}{85}\times 100\\
&\approx -22.4
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-22.4\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(29, 54, 62, 64, 66, 73\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(29, 54, 62, 64, 66, 73\). With an even count of \(6\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{62+64}{2}=63\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: An account recorded these daily new followers: \(58, 21, 75, 11, 11, 85, 11\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(11\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(11\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the strength of two correlations using their absolute values.
questions.question: Relationship A has a Pearson correlation coefficient of r = \(-0.71\), and Relationship B has r = \(-0.24\). Which relationship shows a stronger linear association between its variables?
questions.explanation: Compare \(|r_A|=0.71\) and \(|r_B|=0.24\). Relationship A has the greater magnitude and therefore the stronger linear association. The sign gives direction, not strength.
questions.hint: Compare the absolute values of the coefficients, not their signs.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a described relationship as positive, negative, or no correlation.
questions.question: As advertising spend increases, website traffic tends to increase. What type of relationship does this describe?
questions.explanation: The described variables tend to move in the same direction, giving a positive association. This describes association rather than demonstrating causation.
questions.hint: Positive: both move the same direction. Negative: they move opposite directions. No correlation: no consistent pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An experiment recorded these reaction times (ms): \(63, 59, 37, 19, 83, 68\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(19\) and the maximum is \(83\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=83-19=64\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the first quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: A logistics company recorded these delivery times (hours) (sorted): \(36, 49, 59, 60, 70, 75, 80, 99\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_1\) (the first quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the lower half is \(36, 49, 59, 60\). Its median is \(Q_1=\frac{49+59}{2}=54\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks daily orders for an online store over five months: Jan: \(37\), Feb: \(79\), Mar: \(110\), Apr: \(30\), May: \(97\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(110\), which occurs in Mar.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lowest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(72, 34, 52, 60, 87, 36, 96\). What is the lowest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The lowest value is \(34\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the lowest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the daily new followers recorded at an account. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: B
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains counts or measured quantities, so its values are numerical. Recording these values over time does not change their numerical value type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the number of orders placed by a team for supplies each day. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: A count takes nonnegative whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: A factory recorded these units produced per shift (sorted): \(14, 21, 23, 47, 78, 90, 91, 96\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{21+23}{2}=22\\
Q_3 &= \frac{90+91}{2}=90.5\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=90.5-22=68.5
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a small random sample may miss important variation in a diverse population.
questions.question: A national study of units produced per shift includes \(40\) locations selected uniformly at random from thousands of eligible locations nationwide. Why can this sample still raise concerns about population coverage?

options.label: A
options.text: A very small sample size can still fail to capture the full variability of a large, diverse population

options.label: B
options.text: Random selection always guarantees a perfectly representative sample regardless of size

options.label: C
options.text: Sample size never affects how representative a sample is

questions.explanation: Uniform random selection avoids systematically favoring an eligible location, but a particular sample of \(40\) can miss important population variation by chance. With the same sound design, a larger sample usually reduces sampling variability; it does not automatically repair coverage or measurement bias.
questions.hint: Randomness reduces bias, but sample size affects how reliably the sample reflects the whole population.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a seasonal pattern in repeating time-series data.
questions.question: A website's session durations (minutes) show peaks every December and troughs every February, repeating this pattern every year for five years. What best describes this pattern?
questions.explanation: The peak and trough recur at the same calendar positions over multiple years, so the series has an annual seasonal pattern. This is a repeating component rather than a single fluctuation or a two-variable correlation coefficient.
questions.hint: Look for a pattern that repeats at the same time each cycle (e.g., each year).

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows session durations (minutes) by labeled category for a website: North: \(147\); Desktop: \(127\); Retail: \(44\); Q4: \(78\); West: \(120\). Which labeled category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(147\), belonging to the category labeled North.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a portfolio lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(38, 28, 47, 58\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(38+28+47+58=171\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: In a data analysis exercise about reaction times (ms) for an experiment, a pie chart classifies all recorded observations into \(4\) mutually exclusive categories. The known shares are Category E: \(24\%\); Category A: \(15\%\); Category D: \(17\%\). Category B is unlabeled. What percentage does Category B represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(24+15+17)=44\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a z-score given the mean, standard deviation, and a data value.
questions.question: A class's test scores have a mean of \(90\) and a standard deviation of \(5\). What is the z-score of a value of \(80\)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the stated mean, then divide by the stated positive standard deviation: \(z=\frac{80-90}{5}=-2\). The z-score is dimensionless.
questions.hint: Use \(z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\) with the mean and standard deviation supplied in the question.

questions.concept: Effect of outliers on mean vs. median
questions.learningObjective: Compare recomputed mean and median values before and after adding an extreme recorded observation.
questions.question: An experiment's reaction times (ms) were \(23, 40, 22, 26, 37\), with a mean of \(29.6\). A new observation of \(227\) is added. Treat all listed numbers as recorded observations for this comparison. Which statement matches the changes in the mean and median?

options.label: A
options.text: The median increases sharply; the mean changes only slightly

options.label: B
options.text: The mean increases substantially; the median changes little or stays the same

options.label: C
options.text: Both the mean and median stay exactly the same

questions.explanation: Before addition, the mean is \(29.6\) and the median is \(26\). After adding \(227\), the mean is \(62.50\) (rounded to two decimals) and the median is \(31.5\). The mean increases much more than the median; the median can also remain unchanged.
questions.hint: The mean uses every value's magnitude; the median only depends on order/position.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: An online store recorded the following daily orders over \(7\) periods: \(36, 44, 85, 26, 63, 84, 64\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.

questions.learningObjective: Count how many observations in a dataset satisfy a filter condition.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: An app recorded these app load times (seconds): \(38, 86, 38, 79, 27, 26, 38\). What is the mode?

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population variance of a dataset.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD): \(21, 13, 11, 17, 19\) (mean = \(16.2\)). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population variance (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=16.2\). Sum the squared deviations and divide by the population size:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{(21-16.2)^2+(13-16.2)^2+(11-16.2)^2+(17-16.2)^2+(19-16.2)^2}{5}\\
&= \frac{68.8}{5}=13.76
\end{aligned}\]
Variance is measured in squared measurement units; standard deviation is its square root.
questions.hint: Variance = average of the squared differences between each value and the mean.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the highest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders: \(76, 29, 89, 71, 17, 15\). What is the highest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The highest value is \(89\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the highest one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A website recorded session durations (minutes) of \(119\) in Period \(1\) and \(137\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(137-119=18\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a z-score given the mean, standard deviation, and a data value.
questions.question: An experiment's reaction times (ms) have a mean of \(60\) and a standard deviation of \(10\). What is the z-score of a value of \(70\)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the stated mean, then divide by the stated positive standard deviation: \(z=\frac{70-60}{10}=1\). The z-score is dimensionless.
questions.hint: Use \(z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\) with the mean and standard deviation supplied in the question.

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: A store's monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) has \(Q_1=40.5\) and \(Q_3=69.5\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(127\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: A
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 69.5-40.5=29\\
L &= 40.5-1.5(29)=-3\\
U &= 69.5+1.5(29)=113
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(127\) lies above the upper fence, so it is an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.

questions.concept: Identifying net direction in time-series data

options.text: Net increase from first to last period

options.label: C
options.text: Net decrease from first to last period

questions.explanation: Using the stated endpoint criterion, \(\Delta=67-71=-4\). This is negative, so there is a net decrease. This criterion does not establish a fitted regression trend or statistical significance.
questions.hint: Apply the criterion stated in the question to the first and last observations.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: A campaign recorded these click-through rates (percent): \(49, 43, 45, 41, 39\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?

questions.learningObjective: Identify the chart type that satisfies the explicitly stated encoding requirement.

questions.learningObjective: Select a simple imputation rule that preserves the observed mean under explicit value and task assumptions.
