questions.explanation: A uniform random selection from a complete list of the target population is simple random sampling. It does not restrict selection to passers-by or deliberately sample within separate strata.
questions.hint: Consider whether selection is based on a uniform random draw from a complete list, on predefined subgroups, or on availability.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the bin with the highest frequency in a histogram.
questions.question: A histogram of daily new followers for an account uses measurements rounded to whole numbers. Its inclusive integer bins have these counts: \(0\le x\le 20\): \(30\), \(21\le x\le 40\): \(38\), \(41\le x\le 60\): \(31\), \(61\le x\le 80\): \(37\), \(81\le x\le 100\): \(24\). Which bin contains the most observations?
questions.explanation: Compare the stated bin frequencies. The \(21\le x\le 40\) bin has \(38\) observations, strictly more than every other bin. The stated integer rounding removes gaps between consecutive inclusive integer bins.
questions.hint: Compare the bar heights (counts) across all the bins.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A store recorded monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) of \(134\) in Period \(1\) and \(136\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(136-134=2\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A store logged these monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD): \(26, 41, 44, 50, 66, 87, 91\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(26, 41, 44, 50, 66, 87, 91\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(50\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: A website recorded these session durations (minutes): \(26, 24, 22, 18, 14\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=20.8\). The squared deviations sum to \(92.8\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{92.8}{5}=18.56\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{18.56}\approx 4.31
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Count how many observations in a dataset satisfy a filter condition.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders for \(10\) observations: \(86, 38, 86, 18, 20, 48, 88, 44, 23, 72\). How many observations are greater than \(60\)?
questions.explanation: The values satisfying the strict condition \(x>60\) are \(86, 86, 88, 72\). There are \(4\) such observations.
questions.hint: Go through the list and count how many values are above \(60\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store over five months: Jan: \(96\), Feb: \(114\), Mar: \(99\), Apr: \(143\), May: \(150\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(150\), which occurs in May.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two datasets using population standard deviation as the specified spread measure.
questions.question: Two classes recorded these test scores: Beta: \(48\), \(50\), \(49\), \(52\), \(51\); Lumen: \(72\), \(38\), \(55\), \(65\), \(30\). Using population standard deviation to measure spread, which dataset has greater variability?
questions.explanation: The population variances are Beta: \(2\); Lumen: \(251.6\). Taking square roots preserves their order. Therefore, Lumen has the greater population standard deviation. The comparison concerns spread, not the sizes of the means.
questions.hint: Compare distances from each dataset's own mean using the stated spread measure.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows daily orders by category for an online store: Online: \(83\); South: \(127\); Q3: \(198\); North: \(67\); Desktop: \(33\). Which category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(198\), belonging to the category labeled Q3.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: An experiment recorded these reaction times (ms): \(27, 31, 33, 56, 59, 83\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(27, 31, 33, 56, 59, 83\). With an even count of \(6\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{33+56}{2}=44.5\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what each component of a boxplot represents.
questions.question: A conventional Tukey boxplot is drawn for an experiment's reaction times (ms). Which part of the boxplot represents the median of the data?
questions.explanation: In this conventional boxplot, the line inside the box marks the median. The two box edges mark \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\). The whiskers end at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.hint: Distinguish the box interior, box edges, whisker endpoints, and separately plotted observations.

questions.concept: Identifying net direction in time-series data
questions.learningObjective: Classify the sign of the first-to-last net change in a time series.
questions.question: A factory's units produced per shift over five consecutive periods were: \(69, 67, 65, 66, 69\). For this question, classify the direction by the net change from the first period to the last: positive means an increase, negative means a decrease, and zero means no net change. Which option describes that direction?

options.label: A
options.text: No net change between first and last periods

options.label: B
options.text: Net decrease from first to last period

options.label: C
options.text: Net increase from first to last period

questions.explanation: Using the stated endpoint criterion, \(\Delta=69-69=0\). This is zero, so there is no net change between the endpoints. This criterion does not establish a fitted regression trend or statistical significance.
questions.hint: Apply the criterion stated in the question to the first and last observations.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A logistics company recorded these delivery times (hours): \(14, 17, 17, 17, 78, 33, 29\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(17\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(17\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD): \(86, 15, 59, 43, 65\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(15\) and the maximum is \(86\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=86-15=71\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Recalculate a correct total after identifying a duplicate data entry.
questions.question: A dataset of monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store accidentally contains the entry \(79\) twice due to a data-entry error: \(79, 42, 75, 68, 79\). Source records confirm that one occurrence of the repeated value is a copied record. What is the correct total after removing exactly that one duplicate record?
questions.explanation: Remove one confirmed copy of the \(79\) record. The corrected records are \(42, 75, 68, 79\), with total \(42+75+68+79=264\). Equal values alone are not sufficient grounds for deleting independent records.
questions.hint: Identify and remove the duplicate entry before summing.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a city lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(39, 37, 49, 79\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(39+37+49+79=204\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a data quality issue caused by an inconsistent data type.
questions.question: A spreadsheet column intended to hold numeric values for 'Price' contains the entries \(48.99\), \(21.50\), 'N/A', \(50.00\), \(35.75\). What is the data quality issue here?

options.label: A
options.text: The column has too many entries

options.label: B
options.text: One entry is stored as text instead of a number, which is an inconsistent data type

options.label: C
options.text: The price values are not sorted in order

questions.explanation: The column mixes numbers with a nonnumeric text entry or missing-value marker. That entry must be identified and handled explicitly before numerical analysis. Some tools reject it; others silently omit text, so it does not necessarily cause a calculation error in every spreadsheet.
questions.hint: Look for an entry that doesn't match the expected format of the rest of the column.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the highest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: An app recorded these app load times (seconds): \(59, 77, 43, 50, 97, 60, 81\). What is the highest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The highest value is \(97\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the highest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the daily active user counts (thousands) recorded at a product. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: C
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains counts or measured quantities, so its values are numerical. Recording these values over time does not change their numerical value type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change of a metric across a period.
questions.question: A team's points scored per game changed from \(140\) to \(182\) over one quarter. What was the signed percentage change, rounded to one decimal place?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{182-140}{140}\times 100\\
&=30.0
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(30.0\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change by the starting value, then convert to a percentage.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A factory's units produced per shift went from \(69\) to \(134\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{134-69}{69}\times 100\\
&\approx 94.2
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(94.2\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the exact weight in kilograms of packages booked for shipment through an app. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: Before instrument rounding, the modeled duration or mass can vary continuously over a range. It is continuous numerical data, even though an instrument reports it to finite precision.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: In a data analysis exercise about app load times (seconds) for an app, a pie chart classifies all recorded observations into \(3\) mutually exclusive categories. The known shares are Category E: \(31\%\); Category B: \(12\%\). Category C is unlabeled. What percentage does Category C represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(31+12)=57\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A survey recorded the following customer satisfaction point totals over \(5\) periods: \(40, 56, 14, 25, 40\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(5\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{40+56+14+25+40}{5}\\
&= \frac{175}{5}\\
&=35.00
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the first quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: A factory recorded these units produced per shift (sorted): \(10, 46, 61, 62, 76, 87, 91, 94\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_1\) (the first quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the lower half is \(10, 46, 61, 62\). Its median is \(Q_1=\frac{46+61}{2}=53.5\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the second-highest value in a dataset after sorting.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders: \(110, 69, 47, 143, 70, 77\). What is the second-highest value?
questions.explanation: Sorted from largest to smallest, the observations are \(143, 110, 77, 70, 69, 47\). The second value is \(110\).
questions.hint: Sort the values from largest to smallest, then find the second one.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A city logged these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(14, 22, 26, 54, 66, 74, 80\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(14, 22, 26, 54, 66, 74, 80\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(54\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Select an appropriate first investigation when numeric values are missing.
questions.question: A store's dataset of monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) has a numeric column with \(8\%\) of its values missing, appearing scattered through the records. Which is generally the most reasonable first step?

options.label: A
options.text: Automatically replace every missing value with zero without investigation

options.label: C
options.text: Investigate why the values are missing before deciding to remove or impute them

questions.explanation: First examine why values are absent and whether missingness relates to the measurements or the collection process. The apparent pattern alone does not establish a missing-completely-at-random mechanism. Then choose a treatment appropriate to the analytical task.
questions.hint: Consider what you need to know about the collection process before choosing a numerical treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a groupby-and-aggregate operation produces.
questions.question: A data analyst runs `df.groupby('region')['sales'].mean()` on a sales dataset for a store. Assume region labels are present and sales is numeric, with at least one observed sales value in every group. What does the result represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The average sales value for each region

options.label: B
options.text: The total number of rows for each region

options.label: C
options.text: The overall average sales across the entire dataset

questions.explanation: The operation partitions rows by the region column, then calculates the arithmetic mean of observed numeric sales within each region. The resulting Series has one mean per region; it is neither an overall mean nor a row count. Missing sales values are skipped by the default mean aggregation.
questions.hint: groupby() splits the data into groups first, then the aggregation is applied within each group.

questions.concept: Calculating a percentage of a total
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage share of one category relative to the total.
questions.question: A table lists points scored per game for a team. The regions have nonoverlapping contributions: North: \(45\); West: \(20\); East: \(35\); Central: \(51\); South: \(41\). What percentage of the total does East represent (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The total is \(45+20+35+51+41=192\). The share for East is \(\frac{35}{192}\approx 18.2\%\), rounded to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the category's value by the total, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a scatter plot that shows no clear pattern.
questions.question: A scatter plot of a customer's age versus the amount they spend per order uses two quantitative variables. Its points are scattered with no visible upward or downward linear pattern. What does this suggest about the observed variables?

options.label: A
options.text: There is little to no linear correlation between the variables

options.label: B
options.text: There is a strong positive correlation between the variables

options.label: C
options.text: One variable definitely causes the other

questions.explanation: The described scatter suggests little or no visible linear association in the observed data. It does not establish that the exact correlation is zero, rule out a nonlinear relationship, or prove causation.
questions.hint: A clear correlation would show points following a visible upward or downward pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands) (sorted): \(18, 41, 57, 63, 78, 88, 94, 98\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{41+57}{2}=49\\
Q_3 &= \frac{88+94}{2}=91\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=91-49=42
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD): \(29, 32, 41, 48, 50, 52, 80, 81\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(29, 32, 41, 48, 50, 52, 80, 81\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{48+50}{2}=49\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(24, 23, 13, 24, 24, 59, 17\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(24\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(24\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows delivery times (hours) for a logistics company by month: Jan: \(109\), Feb: \(56\), Mar: \(76\), Apr: \(29\). What value does the bar for Feb show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(56\) to Feb. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the chart type that satisfies the explicitly stated encoding requirement.
questions.question: An analyst wants a chart for showing what percentage of a survey's total customer satisfaction points comes from each of a few categories. The categories are mutually exclusive contributions to one additive total. Which chart uses slices of a circle to display their percentage shares?
questions.explanation: A pie chart encodes shares of one complete total as slices of a circle. A bar chart can also show percentages, but it does not use the requested circle-slice form.
questions.hint: Match the chart type to what's being shown: comparison, trend over time, parts of a whole, relationship between two variables, or a distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish between a population and a sample in a research scenario.
questions.question: A researcher surveys \(30\) people selected uniformly at random from a store workforce of \(1200\) people. Relative to that workforce, does the surveyed group constitute the population or a sample?

options.label: A
options.text: The population consists only of members not selected for this investigation

questions.explanation: The target population is the entire stated group. Only a proper subset is selected, so the surveyed set is a sample from that population.
questions.hint: A population includes every member of the group of interest; a sample is a subset of it.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: An experiment recorded reaction times (ms) of \(67\) in Period \(1\) and \(93\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(93-67=26\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(68, 60, 67, 45, 32\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(32\) and the maximum is \(68\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=68-32=36\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.concept: Combining chart types on a dashboard
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate chart types for different analytical questions on a dashboard.
questions.question: A dashboard needs to show both the month-over-month trend of monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store and how that total breaks down by category in the most recent month. Which combination of charts fits best? Each category contributes a nonoverlapping part of the latest total.

options.label: A
options.text: Two identical line charts showing the same data twice

options.label: B
options.text: A line chart for the trend and a bar or pie chart for the latest breakdown

options.label: C
options.text: A single scatter plot combining both pieces of information

questions.explanation: A line chart supports the time-ordered view. A bar chart compares the latest category contributions; a pie chart is also possible for a few disjoint shares of one whole. These two views answer different dashboard questions.
questions.hint: Different questions (trend vs. breakdown) usually call for different chart types.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the highest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(54, 90, 63, 52, 39, 21, 89, 86\). What is the highest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The highest value is \(90\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the highest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks test scores for a class over five months: Jan: \(77\), Feb: \(20\), Mar: \(92\), Apr: \(126\), May: \(77\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(126\), which occurs in Apr.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows daily orders by labeled category for an online store: East: \(138\); Online: \(182\); Retail: \(87\); Q4: \(158\). Which labeled category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(182\), belonging to the category labeled Online.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sample size given a study description.
questions.question: A researcher wants to study opinions across a population of \(25000\) people and selects \(500\) of them at random to survey. What is the sample size in this study?
questions.explanation: The selected study group contains \(500\) people, so the sample size is \(n=500\). The full population size is \(25000\).
questions.hint: The sample size is how many were actually selected and studied, not the size of the whole group.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the correct way to calculate a mean when a value is missing.
questions.question: A stock's daily stock closing prices (USD) dataset has \(5\) entries, but one entry is missing (blank): \(80, 64, 74, 44\), [missing]. How should the mean of only the four observed values be calculated, without imputing the missing value?

options.label: A
options.text: Use only the four observed values: \(\frac{262}{4}=65.5\).

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the missing value as zero: \(\frac{262}{5}=52.4\).

options.label: C
options.text: No statistic can be calculated from the observed values.

questions.explanation: The requested statistic is the observed-data mean, so divide the observed sum by the observed count: \(\bar{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{262}{4}=65.5\). The mean of all five intended entries cannot be determined without the missing value or an explicit imputation assumption.
questions.hint: Decide which entries belong in the requested statistic and use the matching denominator.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret individually plotted points beyond a boxplot's whiskers.
questions.question: On a Tukey boxplot of an online store's daily orders, several individual points are plotted separately beyond the whiskers. What do these points most likely represent? Here, whiskers stop at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.explanation: Under the stated Tukey convention, observations outside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences are flagged as outliers and plotted separately beyond the whiskers. This flag does not by itself establish a data-entry error.
questions.hint: Compare the positions of the separate points with the interval covered by the whiskers.

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: A survey's customer satisfaction point totals has \(Q_1=44\) and \(Q_3=70\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(121\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

options.label: C
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 70-44=26\\
L &= 44-1.5(26)=5\\
U &= 70+1.5(26)=109
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(121\) lies above the upper fence, so it is an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the number of items or events recorded each day at a campaign. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: C
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains counts or measured quantities, so its values are numerical. Recording these values over time does not change their numerical value type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(40, 34, 46, 32, 38\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=38\). The squared deviations sum to \(120\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{120}{5}=24\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{24}\approx 4.90
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for an app lists these counts across \(5\) categories: \(15, 63, 58, 33, 71\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(15+63+58+33+71=240\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows daily orders for an online store by month: Jan: \(21\), Feb: \(123\), Mar: \(75\), Apr: \(43\). What value does the bar for Mar show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(75\) to Mar. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two datasets using population standard deviation as the specified spread measure.
questions.question: Two classes recorded these test scores: Nova: \(50\), \(51\), \(49\), \(48\), \(52\); Pinnacle: \(38\), \(65\), \(30\), \(55\), \(72\). Using population standard deviation to measure spread, which dataset has greater variability?
questions.explanation: The population variances are Nova: \(2\); Pinnacle: \(251.6\). Taking square roots preserves their order. Therefore, Pinnacle has the greater population standard deviation. The comparison concerns spread, not the sizes of the means.
questions.hint: Compare distances from each dataset's own mean using the stated spread measure.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the number of orders attributed to a marketing campaign each day. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: A count takes nonnegative whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store over five months: Jan: \(148\), Feb: \(139\), Mar: \(104\), Apr: \(144\), May: \(146\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(148\), which occurs in Jan.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded the following daily active user counts (thousands) over \(7\) periods: \(33, 67, 84, 40, 17, 24, 65\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(7\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{33+67+84+40+17+24+65}{7}\\
&= \frac{330}{7}\\
&\approx 47.14
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows patient wait times (minutes) by category for a clinic: Q3: \(110\); East: \(163\); Desktop: \(170\); South: \(169\); Q4: \(68\). Which category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(170\), belonging to the category labeled Desktop.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a described relationship as positive, negative, or no correlation.
questions.question: As a website's page load time increases, its bounce rate tends to increase. What type of relationship does this describe?
questions.explanation: The described variables tend to move in the same direction, giving a positive association. This describes association rather than demonstrating causation.
questions.hint: Positive: both move the same direction. Negative: they move opposite directions. No correlation: no consistent pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A store logged these monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD): \(27, 54, 83, 86, 88\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(27, 54, 83, 86, 88\). There are \(5\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{5+1}{2}=3\): \(83\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: An app's load times (seconds) went from \(125\) to \(97\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{97-125}{125}\times 100\\
&=-22.4
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-22.4\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: An account recorded these daily new followers: \(31, 44, 61, 64, 74, 77, 91, 92\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(31, 44, 61, 64, 74, 77, 91, 92\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{64+74}{2}=69\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A logistics company recorded these delivery times (hours): \(38, 46, 69, 46, 81, 46, 29\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(46\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(46\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for an account lists these counts across \(5\) categories: \(52, 21, 28, 59, 79\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(52+21+28+59+79=239\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A team recorded these points scored per game: \(95, 54, 81, 77, 36\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(36\) and the maximum is \(95\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=95-36=59\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify stratified sampling from a described method.
questions.question: A researcher divides a country's voters into regions, then randomly selects a proportional number of voters from each region to survey. What sampling method is this?
questions.explanation: The researcher partitions the population into strata and randomly samples within every stratum. This is stratified sampling. Proportional allocation is the version used here; stratified sampling does not require proportional allocation in every application.
questions.hint: This method deliberately splits the population into subgroups before sampling from each one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lowest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A factory recorded these units produced per shift: \(50, 45, 14, 38, 21, 67, 38, 91\). What is the lowest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The lowest value is \(14\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the lowest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains customer feedback labels at a product such as 'Poor', 'Fair', 'Good', 'Excellent'. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: B
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains names or category labels, so its values are categorical. It does not contain numerical measurements or a mixture of both value types.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the number of orders placed through an app each day. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: A count takes nonnegative whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a pie chart with many near-equal categories is difficult to compare.
questions.question: A logistics company's dataset has \(20\) categories of recorded deliveries with fairly similar counts covering the complete dataset. Why would a pie chart likely be a poor choice for visualizing it?

options.label: A
options.text: Too many similarly sized slices make the chart cluttered and hard to compare

options.label: B
options.text: Pie charts cannot display more than \(2\) categories at all

options.label: C
options.text: Pie charts can only be used for numerical, not categorical, data

questions.explanation: Many near-equal slices crowd a pie chart and make small differences difficult to compare. A bar chart aligns lengths to a shared baseline, making category comparisons easier.
questions.hint: Think about how easy it is to visually compare many thin slices of similar size.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD) for a store by month: Jan: \(78\), Feb: \(126\), Mar: \(93\), Apr: \(102\). What value does the bar for Jan show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(78\) to Jan. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a small random sample may miss important variation in a diverse population.
questions.question: A national study of app load times (seconds) includes \(40\) locations selected uniformly at random from thousands of eligible locations nationwide. Why can this sample still raise concerns about population coverage?

options.label: A
options.text: A very small sample size can still fail to capture the full variability of a large, diverse population

options.label: B
options.text: Sample size never affects how representative a sample is

options.label: C
options.text: Random selection always guarantees a perfectly representative sample regardless of size

questions.explanation: Uniform random selection avoids systematically favoring an eligible location, but a particular sample of \(40\) can miss important population variation by chance. With the same sound design, a larger sample usually reduces sampling variability; it does not automatically repair coverage or measurement bias.
questions.hint: Randomness reduces bias, but sample size affects how reliably the sample reflects the whole population.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the first quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands) (sorted): \(10, 13, 31, 32, 49, 67, 84, 85\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_1\) (the first quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the lower half is \(10, 13, 31, 32\). Its median is \(Q_1=\frac{13+31}{2}=22\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sampling method used in a research scenario.
questions.question: A researcher studying users of a product surveys only the people who happen to walk by their table today. What sampling method does this describe?
questions.explanation: The researcher recruits easily available passers-by rather than using a random draw from a complete population list. This is convenience sampling; it need not reflect the target population.
questions.hint: Consider whether selection is based on a uniform random draw from a complete list, on predefined subgroups, or on availability.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the bin with the highest frequency in a histogram.
questions.question: A histogram of daily new followers for an account uses measurements rounded to whole numbers. Its inclusive integer bins have these counts: \(0\le x\le 20\): \(16\), \(21\le x\le 40\): \(3\), \(41\le x\le 60\): \(5\), \(61\le x\le 80\): \(33\), \(81\le x\le 100\): \(15\). Which bin contains the most observations?
questions.explanation: Compare the stated bin frequencies. The \(61\le x\le 80\) bin has \(33\) observations, strictly more than every other bin. The stated integer rounding removes gaps between consecutive inclusive integer bins.
questions.hint: Compare the bar heights (counts) across all the bins.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: An experiment recorded the following reaction times (ms) over \(7\) periods: \(83, 61, 79, 73, 26, 66, 90\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(7\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{83+61+79+73+26+66+90}{7}\\
&= \frac{478}{7}\\
&\approx 68.29
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.concept: Identifying net direction in time-series data
questions.learningObjective: Classify the sign of the first-to-last net change in a time series.
questions.question: A team's points scored per game over five consecutive periods were: \(76, 88, 94, 97, 124\). For this question, classify the direction by the net change from the first period to the last: positive means an increase, negative means a decrease, and zero means no net change. Which option describes that direction?

options.label: A
options.text: Net decrease from first to last period

options.label: B
options.text: Net increase from first to last period

options.label: C
options.text: No net change between first and last periods

questions.explanation: Using the stated endpoint criterion, \(\Delta=124-76=48\). This is positive, so there is a net increase. This criterion does not establish a fitted regression trend or statistical significance.
questions.hint: Apply the criterion stated in the question to the first and last observations.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A city logged these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(13, 26, 79, 81, 83\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(13, 26, 79, 81, 83\). There are \(5\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{5+1}{2}=3\): \(79\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores: \(18, 29, 34, 50, 58, 61, 83, 95\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(18, 29, 34, 50, 58, 61, 83, 95\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{50+58}{2}=54\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores: \(46, 34, 82, 16, 46, 46, 79\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(46\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(46\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish between a population and a sample in a research scenario.
questions.question: A researcher surveys all \(20000\) employees at a company about job satisfaction. Take the entire stated group of people or the entire stated batch of items as the target population. Does the inspected or surveyed set include that whole population or only a sample?

options.label: C
options.text: The population consists only of members not selected for this investigation

questions.explanation: The target population is the entire stated group. Every member is included, so the inspected or surveyed set is the full population, and the investigation is a census.
questions.hint: A population includes every member of the group of interest; a sample is a subset of it.

questions.learningObjective: Recalculate a statistic correctly after removing a duplicate record.
questions.question: A logistics company's delivery times (hours) dataset was supposed to have \(5\) distinct records but a duplicate row caused it to have \(6\) entries: \(45, 24, 37, 33, 32, 37\). Source records confirm that the last listed row is a copy of an earlier row; equal values in other distinct records are legitimate. What is the correct mean after removing only that last duplicate row (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation: Keep the first five source-confirmed distinct records: \(45, 24, 37, 33, 32\). Their sum is \(171\), giving \(\bar{x}=\frac{171}{5}=34.20\). Retain any legitimate repeated values among those five records.
questions.hint: Remove the duplicate row first, then recompute the mean on the corrected dataset.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: An account recorded these daily new followers (sorted): \(22, 26, 48, 58, 63, 67, 80, 84\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{26+48}{2}=37\\
Q_3 &= \frac{67+80}{2}=73.5\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=73.5-37=36.5
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a scatter plot that shows no clear pattern.
questions.question: A scatter plot of a phone's mass versus its battery life uses two quantitative variables. Its points are scattered with no visible upward or downward linear pattern. What does this suggest about the observed variables?

options.label: A
options.text: There is little to no linear correlation between the variables

options.label: B
options.text: One variable definitely causes the other

options.label: C
options.text: There is a strong positive correlation between the variables

questions.explanation: The described scatter suggests little or no visible linear association in the observed data. It does not establish that the exact correlation is zero, rule out a nonlinear relationship, or prove causation.
questions.hint: A clear correlation would show points following a visible upward or downward pattern.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: A pie chart divides the total of points scored per game for a team into \(3\) mutually exclusive categories covering the whole total. The known shares are Category B: \(19\%\); Category E: \(14\%\). Category C is unlabeled. What percentage does Category C represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(19+14)=67\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: An experiment's reaction times (ms) has \(Q_1=37\) and \(Q_3=60.5\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(106\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

options.label: B
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 60.5-37=23.5\\
L &= 37-1.5(23.5)=1.75\\
U &= 60.5+1.5(23.5)=95.75
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(106\) lies above the upper fence, so it is an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what each component of a boxplot represents.
questions.question: A conventional Tukey boxplot is drawn for a class's test scores. Which part of the boxplot represents the median of the data?
questions.explanation: In this conventional boxplot, the line inside the box marks the median. The two box edges mark \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\). The whiskers end at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.hint: Distinguish the box interior, box edges, whisker endpoints, and separately plotted observations.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
questions.question: A survey recorded these customer satisfaction point totals: \(21, 35, 27, 31, 33\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=29.4\). The squared deviations sum to \(123.2\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{123.2}{5}=24.64\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{24.64}\approx 4.96
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.concept: Combining chart types on a dashboard
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate chart types for different analytical questions on a dashboard.
questions.question: A dashboard needs to show both the month-over-month trend of daily new followers for an account and how that total breaks down by category in the most recent month. Which combination of charts fits best? Each category contributes a nonoverlapping part of the latest total.

options.label: A
options.text: Two identical line charts showing the same data twice

options.label: B
options.text: A single scatter plot combining both pieces of information

options.label: C
options.text: A line chart for the trend and a bar or pie chart for the latest breakdown

questions.explanation: A line chart supports the time-ordered view. A bar chart compares the latest category contributions; a pie chart is also possible for a few disjoint shares of one whole. These two views answer different dashboard questions.
questions.hint: Different questions (trend vs. breakdown) usually call for different chart types.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A survey recorded these customer satisfaction point totals: \(30, 69, 86, 23, 41, 61\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(23\) and the maximum is \(86\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=86-23=63\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the chart type that satisfies the explicitly stated encoding requirement.
questions.question: An analyst wants a chart for showing how a website's session durations (minutes) changed each month over \(2\) years. Which chart type connects successive monthly points with line segments to emphasize change over time?
questions.explanation: A line chart joins successive time-ordered points, making month-to-month change easy to follow. A bar chart can also display monthly data, but it does not provide the requested connected-point form.
questions.hint: Match the chart type to what's being shown: comparison, trend over time, parts of a whole, relationship between two variables, or a distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the highest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A team recorded these points scored per game: \(76, 28, 65, 75, 19, 89, 67\). What is the highest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The highest value is \(89\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the highest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks daily stock closing prices (USD) for a portfolio over five months: Jan: \(30\), Feb: \(35\), Mar: \(107\), Apr: \(144\), May: \(25\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(144\), which occurs in Apr.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the type of sampling bias present in a research scenario.
questions.question: A survey about running shoe preferences is conducted only at a marathon finish line, asking whoever passes by. The target population is the wider community, not just people at that venue. Which sampling bias is the main concern?

options.label: A
options.text: No bias, since the people were approached at random moments

options.label: B
options.text: Selection bias (the sample overrepresents people already engaged with running)

options.label: C
options.text: Measurement bias due to a faulty survey instrument

questions.explanation: Restricting recruitment to this venue can overrepresent people whose interests or activities are associated with it and underrepresent the wider community. This is selection bias; random timing at a restricted venue does not make the whole-community sample representative.
questions.hint: Consider whether the location or method of choosing participants favors a particular group.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows daily orders by category for an online store: Q3: \(187\); Q2: \(150\); Online: \(47\); South: \(179\); Q1: \(26\). Which category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(187\), belonging to the category labeled Q3.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a campaign lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(73, 68, 41, 78\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(73+68+41+78=260\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two datasets using population standard deviation as the specified spread measure.
questions.question: Two clinics recorded these patient wait times (minutes): Comet: \(50\), \(48\), \(52\), \(49\), \(51\); Drift: \(38\), \(65\), \(72\), \(55\), \(30\). Using population standard deviation to measure spread, which dataset has greater variability?
questions.explanation: The population variances are Comet: \(2\); Drift: \(251.6\). Taking square roots preserves their order. Therefore, Drift has the greater population standard deviation. The comparison concerns spread, not the sizes of the means.
questions.hint: Compare distances from each dataset's own mean using the stated spread measure.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows daily orders for an online store by month: Jan: \(76\), Feb: \(66\), Mar: \(85\), Apr: \(99\), May: \(36\). What value does the bar for Mar show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(85\) to Mar. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a seasonal pattern in repeating time-series data.
questions.question: A team's points scored per game show peaks every December and troughs every February, repeating this pattern every year for five years. What best describes this pattern?
questions.explanation: The peak and trough recur at the same calendar positions over multiple years, so the series has an annual seasonal pattern. This is a repeating component rather than a single fluctuation or a two-variable correlation coefficient.
questions.hint: Look for a pattern that repeats at the same time each cycle (e.g., each year).

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks click counts for a campaign over five months: Jan: \(75\), Feb: \(114\), Mar: \(96\), Apr: \(109\), May: \(148\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(148\), which occurs in May.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Select a simple imputation rule that preserves the observed mean under explicit value and task assumptions.
questions.question: A clinic's column of patient wait times (minutes) has a few missing values, and the rest of the data is roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers. Assume the observed values are positive and not all equal, the missingness is completely at random, and the task only needs a simple descriptive baseline. Which listed fill method preserves the observed column mean after all missing entries are filled?

options.label: A
options.text: Fill every missing value with zero

options.label: B
options.text: Fill the missing values with the column's mean

options.label: C
options.text: Fill the missing values with the maximum value in the column

questions.explanation: Filling each missing entry with the observed mean preserves that mean in the completed column. Positive, nonconstant observed values ensure that zero is below the mean and the maximum is above it, so neither distractor preserves the mean. Mean imputation is only a simple baseline: it reduces variability and does not recover the actual missing measurements or guarantee unbiased downstream inference.
questions.hint: Think about which single value best represents a typical entry when the data has no skew.

questions.concept: Calculating a percentage of a total
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage share of one category relative to the total.
questions.question: A table lists sums of recorded reaction times (ms) for an experiment. The regions have nonoverlapping contributions: East: \(61\); North: \(22\); West: \(55\); Central: \(89\). What percentage of the total does Central represent (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The total is \(61+22+55+89=227\). The share for Central is \(\frac{89}{227}\approx 39.2\%\), rounded to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the category's value by the total, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the third quartile using the median-of-halves convention.
questions.question: A clinic recorded these patient wait times (minutes) (sorted): \(16, 22, 23, 25, 43, 70, 85, 98\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is \(Q_3\) (the third quartile)?
questions.explanation: Under the stated median-of-halves convention, the upper half is \(43, 70, 85, 98\). Its median is \(Q_3=\frac{70+85}{2}=77.5\).
questions.hint: Split the ordered data in half, then find the median of the half you need.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the number of items or events recorded each day at an online store. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains counts or measured quantities, so its values are numerical. Recording these values over time does not change their numerical value type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Recalculate a correct total after identifying a duplicate data entry.
questions.question: A dataset of session durations (minutes) for a website accidentally contains the entry \(60\) twice due to a data-entry error: \(60, 21, 23, 34, 60\). Source records confirm that one occurrence of the repeated value is a copied record. What is the correct total after removing exactly that one duplicate record?
questions.explanation: Remove one confirmed copy of the \(60\) record. The corrected records are \(21, 23, 34, 60\), with total \(21+23+34+60=138\). Equal values alone are not sufficient grounds for deleting independent records.
questions.hint: Identify and remove the duplicate entry before summing.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the exact time in seconds taken by a store checkout process. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: Before instrument rounding, the modeled duration or mass can vary continuously over a range. It is continuous numerical data, even though an instrument reports it to finite precision.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret an SQL query combining a WHERE filter with an aggregate function.
questions.question: A SQL query is written as: `SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;` on an orders table for an ordering app. Assume amount is numeric and at least one order satisfies the filter. What does this query return?

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of orders above \(100\)

options.label: B
options.text: The average order amount across all orders, regardless of amount

options.label: C
options.text: The average order amount, considering only orders above \(100\)

questions.explanation: The WHERE condition keeps only rows with \(\mathrm{amount}>100\). AVG then computes the arithmetic mean of those qualifying amounts, rather than averaging all orders or counting them. Without a qualifying value, SQL AVG would return NULL; the question explicitly excludes that case.
questions.hint: The WHERE clause filters rows before the aggregate function is applied.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a described relationship as positive, negative, or no correlation.
questions.question: As daily exercise time increases, resting heart rate tends to decrease. What type of relationship does this describe?
questions.explanation: The described variables tend to move in opposite directions, giving a negative association. This describes association rather than demonstrating causation.
questions.hint: Positive: both move the same direction. Negative: they move opposite directions. No correlation: no consistent pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded the following test scores over \(5\) periods: \(42, 21, 27, 55, 50\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(5\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{42+21+27+55+50}{5}\\
&= \frac{195}{5}\\
&=39.00
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A city logged these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(25, 49, 55, 92, 94\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(25, 49, 55, 92, 94\). There are \(5\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{5+1}{2}=3\): \(55\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: An online store recorded these daily orders: \(13, 14, 35, 40, 47, 50, 56, 89\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(13, 14, 35, 40, 47, 50, 56, 89\). With an even count of \(8\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{40+47}{2}=43.5\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: A class recorded these test scores: \(15, 12, 69, 15, 29, 15, 28\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(15\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(15\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the sum of values for one group within a dataset.
questions.question: A dataset of daily orders for an online store lists (region:value pairs): East: \(36\); East: \(21\); East: \(25\); South: \(59\); South: \(50\); South: \(17\); West: \(23\); West: \(59\); West: \(10\). What is the total for the West region?
questions.explanation: Keep only records in the West group. Their total is \(23+59+10=92\). Other groups are excluded from this sum.
questions.hint: Add up only the entries labeled West.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interquartile range using median-of-halves quartiles.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit) (sorted): \(14, 19, 32, 41, 73, 79, 80, 92\). Use the median-of-halves method: split the eight ordered values into two halves of four values each. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
questions.explanation:
Using the specified median-of-halves convention:
\[\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{19+32}{2}=25.5\\
Q_3 &= \frac{79+80}{2}=79.5\\
\operatorname{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1=79.5-25.5=54
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the median of each four-value half, then subtract \(Q_1\) from \(Q_3\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a weighted mean when combining groups of different sizes.
questions.question: A city has two groups: Group \(1\) has \(28\) observations with a mean of \(70\), and Group \(2\) has \(32\) observations with a mean of \(74\). What is the overall (weighted) mean across both groups (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
Multiply each group mean by that group count, then divide the combined total by the combined count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{28\cdot 70+32\cdot 74}{28+32}\\
&= \frac{4328}{60}\\
&\approx 72.13
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Multiply each group mean by its number of observations before combining the groups.

questions.learningObjective: Count how many observations in a dataset satisfy a filter condition.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD) for \(10\) observations: \(74, 17, 30, 66, 14, 42, 91, 80, 52, 10\). How many observations are greater than \(70\)?
questions.explanation: The values satisfying the strict condition \(x>70\) are \(74, 91, 80\). There are \(3\) such observations.
questions.hint: Go through the list and count how many values are above \(70\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A city recorded these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(27, 95, 38, 62, 30, 100\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(27\) and the maximum is \(100\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=100-27=73\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows reaction times (ms) by labeled category for an experiment: West: \(139\); East: \(153\); Desktop: \(146\); Q1: \(181\); Q2: \(105\). Which labeled category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(181\), belonging to the category labeled Q1.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A factory recorded units produced per shift of \(103\) in Period \(1\) and \(135\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(135-103=32\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lowest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A logistics company recorded these delivery times (hours): \(93, 66, 54, 27, 31, 92, 14\). What is the lowest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The lowest value is \(14\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the lowest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify stratified sampling from a described method.
questions.question: A researcher divides an online store's customers into loyalty tiers, then randomly selects a proportional number of customers from each loyalty tier to survey. What sampling method is this?
questions.explanation: The researcher partitions the population into strata and randomly samples within every stratum. This is stratified sampling. Proportional allocation is the version used here; stratified sampling does not require proportional allocation in every application.
questions.hint: This method deliberately splits the population into subgroups before sampling from each one.

questions.concept: Effect of outliers on mean vs. median
questions.learningObjective: Compare recomputed mean and median values before and after adding an extreme recorded observation.
questions.question: An app's load times (seconds) were \(33, 28, 33, 31, 36\), with a mean of \(32.2\). A new observation of \(183\) is added. Treat all listed numbers as recorded observations for this comparison. Which statement matches the changes in the mean and median?

options.label: A
options.text: The median increases sharply; the mean changes only slightly

options.label: B
options.text: The mean increases substantially; the median changes little or stays the same

options.label: C
options.text: Both the mean and median stay exactly the same

questions.explanation: Before addition, the mean is \(32.2\) and the median is \(33\). After adding \(183\), the mean is \(57.33\) (rounded to two decimals) and the median is \(33\). The mean increases much more than the median; the median can also remain unchanged.
questions.hint: The mean uses every value's magnitude; the median only depends on order/position.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a portfolio lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(49, 36, 20, 54\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(49+36+20+54=159\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Select a justified verification step for a suspicious numerical observation.
questions.question: A team's points scored per game dataset contains: \(24\), \(37\), \(28\), \(25\), \(240\). The value \(240\) is suspiciously large compared to the rest. What is the most justified next step before deciding how this unusual observation should be treated?

options.label: A
options.text: It could be a data-entry error or a genuine extreme value; verify the source before deciding how to treat it

options.label: B
options.text: Replace it immediately with a typical value because its large magnitude proves a recording error

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the unusual observation immediately without checking its source

questions.explanation: The observation is unusual relative to the other values, so it deserves investigation. A tenfold value can result from a recording mistake, but that pattern alone does not prove the value is erroneous. Verify the source and measurement context before correcting, excluding, or retaining it.
questions.hint: Consider what evidence is needed before changing or excluding an unusual recorded value.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A logistics company's delivery times (hours) went from \(68\) to \(55\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{55-68}{68}\times 100\\
&\approx -19.1
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-19.1\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a small random sample may miss important variation in a diverse population.
questions.question: A national study of monthly revenue (thousands of USD) includes \(40\) locations selected uniformly at random from thousands of eligible locations nationwide. Why can this sample still raise concerns about population coverage?

options.label: A
options.text: Random selection always guarantees a perfectly representative sample regardless of size

options.label: B
options.text: Sample size never affects how representative a sample is

options.label: C
options.text: A very small sample size can still fail to capture the full variability of a large, diverse population

questions.explanation: Uniform random selection avoids systematically favoring an eligible location, but a particular sample of \(40\) can miss important population variation by chance. With the same sound design, a larger sample usually reduces sampling variability; it does not automatically repair coverage or measurement bias.
questions.hint: Randomness reduces bias, but sample size affects how reliably the sample reflects the whole population.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains the names of websites in a directory. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains names or category labels, so its values are categorical. It does not contain numerical measurements or a mixture of both value types.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.concept: Outlier detection with the IQR rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a recorded observation lies outside either of the two 1.5-IQR fences.
questions.question: An app's load times (seconds) has \(Q_1=46\) and \(Q_3=68.5\). Using the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) rule, is an observation of \(57\) an outlier? A value is an outlier only if it is strictly below \(Q_1-1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) or strictly above \(Q_3+1.5\operatorname{IQR}\).

options.label: A
options.text: No, it is not an outlier

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be determined without the full dataset

questions.explanation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IQR} &= 68.5-46=22.5\\
L &= 46-1.5(22.5)=12.25\\
U &= 68.5+1.5(22.5)=102.25
\end{aligned}\]
The observation \(57\) lies within the two fences, so it is not an outlier.
questions.hint: Calculate both fences and compare the observation with the entire permitted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population standard deviation of a small dataset.
