questions.question: A clinic recorded these patient wait times (minutes): \(23, 25, 37, 29, 33\). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population standard deviation (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=29.4\). The squared deviations sum to \(131.2\). Divide by the population size and take the square root:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{131.2}{5}=26.24\\
\sigma &= \sqrt{26.24}\approx 5.12
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Find the mean, average the squared deviations from it (variance), then take the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population variance of a dataset.
questions.question: An experiment recorded these reaction times (ms): \(28, 22, 24, 30, 20\) (mean = \(24.8\)). Treat the listed values as the entire population. What is the population variance (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation:
The population mean is \(\mu=24.8\). Sum the squared deviations and divide by the population size:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{(28-24.8)^2+(22-24.8)^2+(24-24.8)^2+(30-24.8)^2+(20-24.8)^2}{5}\\
&= \frac{68.8}{5}=13.76
\end{aligned}\]
Variance is measured in squared measurement units; standard deviation is its square root.
questions.hint: Variance = average of the squared differences between each value and the mean.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the bin with the highest frequency in a histogram.
questions.question: A histogram of daily orders for an online store uses measurements rounded to whole numbers. Its inclusive integer bins have these counts: \(0\le x\le 20\): \(17\), \(21\le x\le 40\): \(16\), \(41\le x\le 60\): \(23\), \(61\le x\le 80\): \(31\), \(81\le x\le 100\): \(18\). Which bin contains the most observations?
questions.explanation: Compare the stated bin frequencies. The \(61\le x\le 80\) bin has \(31\) observations, strictly more than every other bin. The stated integer rounding removes gaps between consecutive inclusive integer bins.
questions.hint: Compare the bar heights (counts) across all the bins.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the type of sampling bias present in a research scenario.
questions.question: A survey about smartphone preferences is conducted only at an electronics store, asking whoever passes by. The target population is the wider community, not just people at that venue. Which sampling bias is the main concern?

options.label: A
options.text: No bias, since the people were approached at random moments

options.label: B
options.text: Measurement bias due to a faulty survey instrument

options.label: C
options.text: Selection bias (electronics-store visitors may differ from the wider community in smartphone interests)

questions.explanation: Restricting recruitment to this venue can overrepresent people whose interests or activities are associated with it and underrepresent the wider community. This is selection bias; random timing at a restricted venue does not make the whole-community sample representative.
questions.hint: Consider whether the location or method of choosing participants favors a particular group.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish discrete numerical data from continuous numerical data.
questions.question: A dataset records the number of orders placed through a website each day. Treat exact physical measurements as idealized values before instrument rounding. How should the recorded variable be classified?
questions.explanation: A count takes nonnegative whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data.
questions.hint: Discrete data is countable in whole units; continuous data can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a data quality issue caused by an inconsistent data type.
questions.question: A spreadsheet column intended to hold numeric values for 'Weight (kg)' contains the entries \(34.2\), \(17.5\), 'heavy', \(7.1\), \(36.8\). What is the data quality issue here?

options.label: A
options.text: One entry is stored as text instead of a number, which is an inconsistent data type

options.label: B
options.text: The weight (kg) values are not sorted in order

options.label: C
options.text: The column has too many entries

questions.explanation: The column mixes numbers with a nonnumeric text entry or missing-value marker. That entry must be identified and handled explicitly before numerical analysis. Some tools reject it; others silently omit text, so it does not necessarily cause a calculation error in every spreadsheet.
questions.hint: Look for an entry that doesn't match the expected format of the rest of the column.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what each component of a boxplot represents.
questions.question: A conventional Tukey boxplot is drawn for a team's points scored per game. Which part of the boxplot represents the median of the data?
questions.explanation: In this conventional boxplot, the line inside the box marks the median. The two box edges mark \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\). The whiskers end at the most extreme observed values inside the \(1.5\operatorname{IQR}\) fences.
questions.hint: Distinguish the box interior, box edges, whisker endpoints, and separately plotted observations.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a small numeric dataset.
questions.question: A survey recorded the following customer satisfaction point totals over \(7\) periods: \(89, 10, 33, 35, 25, 39, 16\). What is the arithmetic mean, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Add the \(7\) recorded values, then divide by their count:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= \frac{89+10+33+35+25+39+16}{7}\\
&= \frac{247}{7}\\
&\approx 35.29
\end{aligned}\]
questions.hint: Add every value together, then divide by how many values there are.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an odd number of values.
questions.question: A city logged these daily high temperatures (degrees Fahrenheit): \(30, 33, 59, 72, 74, 75, 94\). What is the median value?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(30, 33, 59, 72, 74, 75, 94\). There are \(7\) values, so the median is the value in position \(\frac{7+1}{2}=4\): \(72\).
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then find the one exactly in the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the second-highest value in a dataset after sorting.
questions.question: A campaign recorded these click counts: \(85, 66, 34, 141, 106, 97\). What is the second-highest value?
questions.explanation: Sorted from largest to smallest, the observations are \(141, 106, 97, 85, 66, 34\). The second value is \(106\).
questions.hint: Sort the values from largest to smallest, then find the second one.

questions.learningObjective: Find the median of an ordered dataset with an even number of values.
questions.question: A store recorded these monthly revenue figures (thousands of USD): \(15, 17, 26, 44, 56, 90\). What is the median?
questions.explanation: The ordered data are \(15, 17, 26, 44, 56, 90\). With an even count of \(6\), average the two middle values: \(\operatorname{median}=\frac{26+44}{2}=35\).
questions.hint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Read a specific data value directly from a bar chart.
questions.question: A bar chart shows app load times (seconds) for an app by month: Jan: \(78\), Feb: \(84\), Mar: \(82\), Apr: \(131\), May: \(115\). What value does the bar for May show?
questions.explanation: The provided month-value pairs assign \(115\) to May. That is the value of the requested bar.
questions.hint: Use the supplied month-value pairs and locate the month named in the question.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
questions.question: An investment analyst recorded these daily stock closing prices (USD): \(61, 79, 35, 32, 32, 32, 15\). What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value \(32\) occurs \(3\) times. Every other value occurs fewer times, so \(32\) is the unique mode.
questions.hint: Look for the value that appears most often in the list.

questions.concept: Finding a missing percentage in a pie chart
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing category's percentage given that pie-chart shares sum to 100%.
questions.question: A pie chart divides the total of daily active users (thousands) for a product into \(3\) mutually exclusive categories covering the whole total. The known shares are Category E: \(14\%\); Category C: \(34\%\). Category D is unlabeled. What percentage does Category D represent?
questions.explanation: The category shares cover the whole pie, so they sum to \(100\%\). The missing share is \(100-(14+34)=52\) percent.
questions.hint: All the slices of a pie chart must add up to \(100\%\).

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a groupby-and-aggregate operation produces.
questions.question: A data analyst runs `df.groupby('region')['sales'].mean()` on a sales dataset for city businesses. Assume region labels are present and sales is numeric, with at least one observed sales value in every group. What does the result represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of rows for each region

options.label: B
options.text: The average sales value for each region

options.label: C
options.text: The overall average sales across the entire dataset

questions.explanation: The operation partitions rows by the region column, then calculates the arithmetic mean of observed numeric sales within each region. The resulting Series has one mean per region; it is neither an overall mean nor a row count. Missing sales values are skipped by the default mean aggregation.
questions.hint: groupby() splits the data into groups first, then the aggregation is applied within each group.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the range (max minus min) of a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A website recorded these session durations (minutes): \(95, 99, 95, 24, 27, 67\). What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: The minimum is \(24\) and the maximum is \(99\). Therefore, \(\operatorname{range}=99-24=75\).
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.concept: Calculating a percentage of a total
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage share of one category relative to the total.
questions.question: A table lists test scores for a class. The regions have nonoverlapping contributions: South: \(63\); West: \(98\); East: \(49\); Central: \(22\). What percentage of the total does South represent (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The total is \(63+98+49+22=232\). The share for South is \(\frac{63}{232}\approx 27.2\%\), rounded to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the category's value by the total, then multiply by \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numeric change in a value between two time periods.
questions.question: A campaign recorded click counts of \(129\) in Period \(1\) and \(91\) in Period \(2\). What is the change from Period \(1\) to Period \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The signed change is the later value minus the earlier value: \(91-129=-38\). A positive result means an increase; a negative result means a decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier period's value from the later period's value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the chart type that satisfies the explicitly stated encoding requirement.
questions.question: An analyst wants a chart for showing what percentage of a team's total points scored per game comes from each of a few categories. The categories are mutually exclusive contributions to one additive total. Which chart uses slices of a circle to display their percentage shares?
questions.explanation: A pie chart encodes shares of one complete total as slices of a circle. A bar chart can also show percentages, but it does not use the requested circle-slice form.
questions.hint: Match the chart type to what's being shown: comparison, trend over time, parts of a whole, relationship between two variables, or a distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Classify the strength and direction of a correlation from its coefficient r.
questions.question: For this exercise, classify Pearson correlation strength as weak when \(|r|<0.4\), moderate when \(0.4\le |r|<0.8\), and strong when \(0.8\le |r|\le 1\). The coefficient is \(r=-0.3\). How should this correlation be described?
questions.explanation: Using the stated exercise rubric, \(|r|=0.3\) gives the strength classification. The negative sign gives the direction, so the answer is weak negative correlation. These cutoffs are an exercise convention, not universal subject-independent thresholds.
questions.hint: Apply the stated magnitude intervals to \(|r|\), then use the sign of \(r\) for direction.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the period with the highest value on a line chart.
questions.question: A line chart tracks test scores for a class over five months: Jan: \(30\), Feb: \(92\), Mar: \(62\), Apr: \(142\), May: \(34\). In which month was the value highest?
questions.explanation: The highest plotted value is \(142\), which occurs in Apr.
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line and check which month it lines up with.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lowest value in a numeric dataset.
questions.question: A product recorded these daily active user counts (thousands): \(68, 32, 12, 24, 57, 58, 42\). What is the lowest value in the dataset?
questions.explanation: Compare every stated observation. The lowest value is \(12\).
questions.hint: Compare every value to find the lowest one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the category with the highest value in a data table.
questions.question: A table shows daily new followers by category for an account: Q4: \(177\); West: \(75\); Q2: \(125\); Q1: \(167\). Which category has the highest value?
questions.explanation: Compare all the stated category values. The unique maximum is \(177\), belonging to the category labeled Q4.
questions.hint: Scan the table and compare each value to find the largest one.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a dataset as categorical or numerical.
questions.question: A dataset contains customer feedback labels at a class such as 'Poor', 'Fair', 'Good', 'Excellent'. Considering only the values in the described column, how should they be classified?

options.label: B
options.text: a mixture of numerical and categorical values

questions.explanation: The column contains names or category labels, so its values are categorical. It does not contain numerical measurements or a mixture of both value types.
questions.hint: Ask whether the values are measured quantities or category labels.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total number of observations from a frequency table.
questions.question: A frequency table for a class lists these counts across \(4\) categories: \(39, 51, 46, 66\). Each observation belongs to exactly one listed category. What is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Because the categories are disjoint and cover the observations, add their frequencies: \(39+51+46+66=202\).
questions.hint: Add up every count shown in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change between two values.
questions.question: A website's session durations (minutes) went from \(120\) to \(87\). What is the percentage change (rounded to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation:
Use the original value as the denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
p &= \frac{87-120}{120}\times 100\\
&=-27.5
\end{aligned}\]
The signed percentage change is \(-27.5\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in value by the original value, then multiply by \(100\).
